substeps.caption: From the VLM to the atomizer: the MiR250 carries the four charged 5N Al cups, 156.7 g of Al-10Si (Si powder under each plug), to the AMAZEMET rePowder. Four charges is how the lab loads the crucible; its own Al runs were 169-180 g (DAL #159).

From the VLM to the atomizer: the MiR250 carries the four charged 5N Al cups, 156.7 g of Al-10Si (Si powder under each plug), to the AMAZEMET rePowder. Four charges is how the lab loads the crucible; its own Al runs were 169-180 g (DAL #159).

The lid is held down by one over-centre draw latch on the furnace's front right, its keeper on the lid, set just tight enough that the seal doesn't hiss (the lab's training video T4, 5:17). The machine's own locking bolt beside it is back: the furnace is at atmosphere. The arm takes the lever by a pull tab.

Pulled out over centre, the lever lets the loop off the keeper. Not measured: about 100 N, 200 N for a stiff one (cover latches of this kind). Pulled that hard, the MiR250 and its arm would tip at 466 N and slide at 505 N; with a 95 kg steel plate under the cabinet, at 730 and 785 N.

The first pump-down starts. As the furnace leaves atmosphere, the machine's bolt comes out in front of the latch's lever: the lid can't be opened under vacuum or pressure (AMAZEMET, install call).

Cut open at the furnace axis; the two back cups are cut through their own axes. Three cycles of pumping down to 4×10⁻¹ mbar and back-filling with 5N argon take the oxygen under 50 ppm. On each pump-down the air under the plugs leaves through their 1/16 in vents (#104).

Still by hand: building this stack. The graphite crucible's threaded shank runs down into the chamber, where a thin graphite nut goes on from below, through the chamber's door, while someone holds the crucible still at the top: "snug but never forced" (the lab's SOP). A robot would need a tool at each end and fine force sensing: the UR10e's own is good to ±5.5 N and ±0.5 N·m; a wrist sensor resolves 0.1 N and 0.005 N·m (Robotiq FT 300-S) or 1/16 N and 1/752 N·m (ATI Mini45). notes/crucible_automation.md

The 10 kW, 7 kHz coil heats the graphite and the graphite the charge. The Type N thermocouple sits in the crucible wall, so the metal lags its reading. The cups glow, then slump into a pool round the rod (Al-10Si is liquid above about 595 °C; a 750 °C hold is assumed).

Real footage, Oct 27 2026, through the furnace port: the four bronze pieces stand round the sealing rod and glow (youtu.be/2brsz-90seg, DAL #219). 630 bronze at 1300 °C, not Al-10Si.
A few minutes on, the pieces sink into their own melt round the rod (2brsz-90seg, about 4:36; at 3:55 Gage says "It's melting in right now").
The charge fully molten, a bright pool round the sealing rod (2brsz-90seg, DAL #219).

Vibration on, then 200 mbar of argon over-pressure on the furnace: the pour runs on the pressure, not the melt's weight (#222). Sealing rod up: the stream falls through the nozzle onto the vibrating plate.

Droplets fly off the plate, freeze in the argon and run down the cone into the container. AMAZEMET's training fits a 0.7 mm nozzle for Al alloys (0.5 mm standard); which one our unit has is not known (#222).

Real footage, from Sterling Baird's MS&T 2026 talk (youtu.be/YmvaeqOQAU4, 4:58): a melt stream, a line of drops, falls onto the tip of the vibrating plate and breaks up into a spray of droplets. The talk doesn't name the alloy or the run.
Real footage, Oct 27 2026, through the view port: the bronze jet lands on the tip of the W-coated carbon-fibre plate and atomizes (2brsz-90seg). 91 % of the 1,080 g became usable powder (DAL #219).
The powder collects in the container under the chamber's valve, still under argon. At the Oct 27 bronze run's yield, 91 % usable (DAL #219), the four cups make about 143 g of powder.
The crucible runs empty; vibration and the coil off, the sealing rod down.
Real photo: the Oct 27 bronze powder as it came out of the atomizer, not yet sieved: lot k7m2q9 (DAL #219). It is sieved in chapter 3.
Real photo: the Oct 22 Al 4047 run, lot c3k0n5, 169 g in, as collected that day: a bag of splats and a jar of powder (Ronnie Guymon, DAL #159).
Closed again. The chamber's valve and the container's own valve are shut, so the powder comes off under argon; the flange clamp opens and the MiR comes back to the container.

How much powder: the four cups make about 26 g of the MIDI's 20-63 um cut, at the Oct 27 run's 17 % under 63 um (DAL #219). The crucible takes much more: filled as on Oct 27, about 385 g of Al (65 g of the cut), and the 400 cm³ one about 684 g (116 g). A 440 g MIDI build then takes 17, 7 or 4 runs.
Done: the powder, not yet sieved, is on the MiR250 in front of the rePowder. Next: the sieving cell and the printer.
